name: Château de Beaucastel Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2016
text:
## Château de Beaucastel Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2016

**The story.** [Beaucastel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel) is one of the most famous names in [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC). It sits at the far northern tip of the appellation, near the village of [Courthézon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Beaucastel,+Courth%C3%A9zon,+France&t=k), where the [mistral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral_%28wind%29) blows hardest. It is also one of the very few estates that grows all thirteen of the appellation's traditional grape varieties and puts every one of them into its red ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel)). The same family has owned it since 1909. Today it is led by Jean-Pierre and François Perrin, the sons of Jacques Perrin, with the fifth generation (Marc, Pierre, Thomas, Cécile, Charles, Matthieu and César) working alongside them ([the estate's history](https://www.beaucastel.com/en/pages/notre-histoire)). The family also co-founded [Tablas Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablas_Creek_Vineyard) in California and partnered on the [Miraval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Miraval) rosé in Provence ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vineyard and how it's made.** The estate describes about 110 hectares in a single block at the north of the appellation ([2019 technical sheet](https://m.familleperrin.com/RW007F/get/print)), with the classic Châteauneuf soil: big rounded stones, the [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), on the surface, with clay, sand and limestone underneath. The stones soak up the day's heat and give it back to the vines at night ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). You can see them from above in the vineyards around the [château](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Beaucastel,+Courth%C3%A9zon,+France&t=k). Beaucastel has farmed [organically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming) since the mid-20th century, so the old vines have sent their roots deep.

Each variety is picked by hand on its own. [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah) and [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) ferment in conical wooden vats; the other varieties in concrete and enamelled stoneware vats. After the [malolactic fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malolactic_fermentation) the family blends them, and the wine then spends a year in large old oak casks (foudres) before bottling ([technical sheet](https://m.familleperrin.com/RW007F/get/print)).

The 2016 blend, as Jeb Dunnuck reported on the day it was bottled: 30% [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre), 30% [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), 10% [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), 10% [Counoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counoise), and the rest a mix of the other permitted varieties ([JJ Buckley, critics' notes](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2016-chateau-de-beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape/2016-453-750/)). That much Mourvèdre is unusual for Châteauneuf, where most wines are mainly Grenache ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). It is what gives Beaucastel its darker, meatier, longer-lived character.

**The vintage.** 2016 is one of the great modern years in the southern Rhône. [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) quotes [Michel Chapoutier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapoutier) saying it could be better than the legendary 1990. Warm conditions all year and reduced yields gave wines of great concentration in colour, tannin and flavour: "certainly one of the great vintages" for reds, and a safe cellaring prospect into the 2030s. At Beaucastel, Marc Perrin told Jeff Leve he thought the 2016 was the best wine the estate had made since the famous back-to-back 1989 and 1990 ([JJ Buckley, critics' notes](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2016-chateau-de-beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape/2016-453-750/)).

**What the critics say for 2016.** As listed by [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2016-chateau-de-beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape/2016-453-750/):
- **[James Suckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Suckling) (Nick Stock): 99** (August 2018). "A stunning Beaucastel. A classic!" Fruit from red through blue to black, with dark stony minerals, spice, wild flowers and herbs; fleshy, impeccably balanced, with silky tannins and decades ahead of it.
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 98** (September 2018). Pepper, leaf, wet earth, spice, dark cherry and plum; polished, deep and fresh. He was sure it is better than both the 1989 and the 1990, and expects it to age for decades.
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 97** (Joe Czerwinski, September 2018). Tasted a week after bottling and he was "blown away": full-bodied, creamy and lush, with raspberry, [garrigue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrigue) and spice. He expected it to go through open and closed phases, and advised trying a bottle rather than forgetting the whole case in storage.
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 97** (James Molesworth, May 2019). Youthfully reserved, warm and polished: cassis, raspberry and cherry, with red licorice, warm stone and singed cedar. "Sock this away in the cellar." Best 2023 to 2040.
- **[Decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decanter_%28magazine%29): 96** (October 2017). Tight on the nose, with fresh black fruit and a herbal seam; full-bodied but lifted, with a dense lattice of ripe tannins. "A truly excellent Beaucastel." Drinking window 2023 to 2039.
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck): 96+** (August 2018). Ripe, sexy and rounded at first, then more structure and minerality: blackberries, blueberries, smoked earth, violets and garrigue. He advised 5 to 7 years in bottle and two decades of life, and said it reminded him of the 2001.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.8** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is ten years old. Dunnuck's 5 to 7 years have passed, Wine Spectator's and Decanter's windows opened in 2023, and your CellarTracker list gives 2025 to 2040. So it is just entering its prime and has a long life ahead. Beaucastel is famous for going quiet for a few years in middle age, as Czerwinski warned, so if a bottle seems closed, give it a long decant (2 to 3 hours). If you have several bottles, keep some for the 2030s.

One thing to know: Beaucastel often has a slightly farmyard, leathery note. Some of it comes from a yeast called [Brettanomyces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brettanomyces), common in Mourvèdre-rich wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel)). Many people love it as part of the style; others find it too much. It tends to grow with age.

**Serving.** The estate suggests about 15°C, cooler than room temperature, and [decanting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) if you can ([technical sheet](https://m.familleperrin.com/RW007F/get/print)). [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/) suggests 2 to 3 hours in a decanter for young vintages. For this vintage today, I'd decant it about 2 hours ahead and serve it in a large, rounded glass.

**Food.** [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/) suggests classic meat dishes: lamb, beef, veal, pork, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, stews, sausages and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet), plus mushrooms and even tuna. My picks: a [leg of lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamb_and_mutton) roasted with garlic and rosemary, [duck confit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_confit), a Provençal beef [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube), or a wild-mushroom dish. I'd avoid delicate white fish and very spicy food, which would fight with the tannin and the alcohol.

**Value and where to buy.** The 2016 is now found mainly at auction and with fine-wine merchants such as [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2016-chateau-de-beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape/2016-453-750/). In the latest store lists on this site, BC Liquor carries the 2020 at $105.99 and the 2019 in magnum at $219.99, and ZYN in Calgary has several recent vintages from $93 to $137. A 2016, from one of the estate's greatest years, is a bottle to treasure.

**From the history books**
- **The Pope's new castle.** Châteauneuf-du-Pape means "the Pope's new castle". In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V), a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) drank the wine from the villages to the north, improved the vineyards and built the [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that is now the appellation's symbol. The wine became known as "Vin du Pape" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **A nobleman's barn.** Beaucastel's own story begins in 1549, when Pierre de Beaucastel bought a barn at [Coudoulet](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Coudoulet+de+Beaucastel,+Courth%C3%A9zon,+France&t=k), land that still belongs to the estate. In 1687 [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV) named a descendant, also Pierre de Beaucastel, "Captain of the Town of Courthézon", in a letter signed by the King and his minister [Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Colbert) ([the estate's history](https://www.beaucastel.com/en/pages/notre-histoire)). Vines are first mentioned for certain in the early 19th century ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel)).
- **Phylloxera and a Suez Canal engineer.** When the [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight) louse wiped out the vineyards in the late 19th century, the owner, Élie Dussaud, sold rather than replant ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel)). [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/) says Dussaud had worked alongside [Ferdinand de Lesseps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_de_Lesseps), the builder of the [Suez Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Canal). In 1909 Pierre Tramier bought the estate and replanted it. His son-in-law Pierre Perrin, a scientist, modernised it, and Jacques Perrin led it until 1978 ([the estate's history](https://www.beaucastel.com/en/pages/notre-histoire)).
- **France's first appellation rules.** Before the First World War, much Châteauneuf was shipped to Burgundy as "vin de médecine" to beef up thinner wines. Fraud became so common that in 1923 local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules. They became law on 15 May 1936, when Châteauneuf was among the first six appellations created. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both [lavender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavandula) and [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Into the modern age.** Around 1990 the Perrins founded [Tablas Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablas_Creek_Vineyard) in [Paso Robles](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Tablas+Creek+Vineyard,+Paso+Robles,+California,+USA&t=k), California, with importer Robert Haas, planting Rhône varieties there. In 2006 they joined [Primum Familiae Vini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primum_Familiae_Vini), a small club of great family wine estates ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Beaucastel)). From the 2009 vintage, Beaucastel was one of the first wines outside [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine) to be sold through the Bordeaux merchants' network, the "Place de Bordeaux" ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **Chamomile tea for the vines.** In the 2019 heat wave, Beaucastel sprayed herbal teas of [chamomile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamomile) on the leaves to help the vines cope. The estate credits this, partly, for the vines suffering little from drought ([technical sheet](https://m.familleperrin.com/RW007F/get/print)).
- **A 20-second hot bath.** According to [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/), Beaucastel briefly heats some grapes, mainly Grenache and mostly in difficult years, to about 80°C for around 20 seconds and then cools them to 20°C before fermenting. The aim is to deactivate enzymes that cause oxidation, keeping the fruit fresh. It isn't pasteurisation.
- **Mourvèdre from Bandol.** Much of Beaucastel's Mourvèdre came from cuttings taken at [Domaine Tempier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Domaine+Tempier&go=Go) in [Bandol](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Domaine+Tempier,+Le+Plan+du+Castellet,+France&t=k), the most famous Mourvèdre estate in France ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954 the Châteauneuf council, amid local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), passed a decree banning "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. It is still in force ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)), and [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard)'s Californian Rhône-style wine, made since 1984, is named [Le Cigare Volant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard) ("flying cigar") after the tale.
- **A cellar to match.** In the 1980s Beaucastel built what was then the largest underground cellar in the Rhône Valley ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/beaucastel-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
